learningObjectives.text: Extract at least two genuinely separate functions from an existing working program
Give each function a name specific enough to describe its one job
Verify the refactored program still produces the exact same output as before

contentSections.body: The Module 3 lab produced a working program: a loop over a real list, building up one summary value. It works, but it's one long block — nothing in it is reusable, nothing in it can be tested on its own, and nothing in it has a name more specific than "the whole program." This lab turns that block into a set of small functions that do the exact same job, better organized.

contentSections.title: Refactor a loop project into functions
contentSections.brief: Start from your Module 3 lab (or write a similar short program now: a real list, a loop, an accumulated summary). Identify the distinct jobs buried inside it — computing something, deciding something, formatting something for display — and pull each one out into its own named function, so the final program calls small, single-job functions instead of running one undivided block.
contentSections.deliverable: The same program, rewritten as named functions, still working.

stages.title: Save the original output
stages.instructions: Run your existing program (or a fresh version of it) and write down its exact printed output somewhere safe — this is what the refactored version has to match exactly, at the end. Then list, in plain English, every distinct job the program is doing: looping, accumulating, deciding something, formatting text, printing.
stages.checkpoint: You have the original program's exact output saved, and a plain-English list of every distinct job it performs.

stages.title: Extract each job into its own function
stages.instructions: Write one function per job from your list — each with a specific name and, where it makes sense, a return value instead of a console.log inside it. At minimum, pull the accumulation logic into its own function that takes the list and returns the summary value, and pull any formatting into a separate function that takes the summary and returns a labeled string.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least two separate functions, each doing exactly one job from your list, each named specifically enough to describe that job.

stages.title: Wire the functions together and check the output matches
stages.instructions: Rewrite the main part of your program to call your new functions in sequence — pass the list into the accumulator function, pass its result into the formatter function, print the formatted result. Run it and compare the output character-for-character against what you saved in stage 1.
stages.checkpoint: The refactored program prints output that exactly matches the original, using your new functions instead of one undivided block.

rubric.criterion: At least two genuinely separate jobs were extracted
rubric.meets: Two or more functions exist, each doing one distinct job (not the same job split arbitrarily in half).

rubric.criterion: Each function has a specific, honest name
rubric.meets: A stranger could guess what each function does from its name alone, with no "and" hiding two jobs in one.

rubric.criterion: At least one function returns a value instead of just printing
rubric.meets: A function that computes something hands its result back with return, rather than only console.log-ing it.

rubric.criterion: The refactored program's output matches the original exactly
rubric.meets: Running the new version produces the same printed result, word for word, as the original saved in stage 1.

rubric.criterion: The main program reads as a sequence of function calls
rubric.meets: The final block calls the new functions in order, rather than repeating their logic inline.

contentSections.body: Refactoring into functions doesn't change what a program does — it changes how easy the same behavior is to read, reuse, and trust.

title: Checkpoint — Functions
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Doing Things Repeatedly, two reaching back further into Making Decisions and Variables and Types. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between a parameter and an argument?

options.label: There's no real difference, the words are interchangeable
A parameter is the placeholder name in the definition; an argument is the real value supplied at the call
A parameter is required, an argument is optional

questions.explanation: The parameter is the reusable placeholder name written in the function's own parentheses. The argument is the specific value handed in at a particular call — different every time, matched to parameters by position.

questions.prompt: What does a function return when it has no return statement at all?

options.label: Calling it throws an error
undefined
Whatever it most recently console.log-ed

questions.explanation: Every function call produces a value. With no explicit return statement, that value is always undefined — regardless of anything the function printed along the way.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't console.log(...) inside a function make its result usable by the code that called it?

options.label: console.log only displays a value for a human to read; only return hands a value back to the caller
console.log actually does return automatically, most of the time
It does make the value usable — that's what console.log is for

questions.explanation: console.log and return are two unrelated actions. Displaying a value on screen and handing it back to the calling code are different things, and only return does the second one.

questions.prompt: What's a strong signal, in a function's own name, that it might be doing more than one job?

options.label: It's longer than one word
It contains "and", joining two separate verbs
It starts with a lowercase letter

questions.explanation: A name honestly describing one job rarely needs "and" — a name like checkAndLogSymptom is confessing, in its own text, that it's doing at least two separate things.

questions.prompt: From Doing Things Repeatedly: what causes a while loop to run forever?

options.label: Using while instead of for
Nothing inside the loop's body ever changes the value the condition depends on
The starting value is too high

questions.explanation: If nothing inside the loop moves the checked value toward making the condition false, the condition stays true forever, and the loop never stops.

questions.prompt: From Doing Things Repeatedly: what's the difference between break and continue?

options.label: break exits the whole loop immediately; continue skips just the current pass and keeps looping
They do the same thing
break is only for while loops, continue is only for for loops

questions.explanation: break stops the loop entirely, right now. continue skips only the rest of the current pass and lets the loop carry on to the next item.

questions.prompt: From Doing Things Repeatedly: why does declaring an accumulator inside a loop's body (instead of before it) break a running total?

options.label: It doesn't — placement inside or outside the loop has no effect
It resets the accumulator to its starting value on every single pass
It makes the loop run one extra time

questions.explanation: A variable declared inside the loop body is recreated fresh on every pass, wiping out whatever it accumulated on the previous one.

questions.prompt: From Doing Things Repeatedly: how many times does `for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++)` run its body?
questions.explanation: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five distinct values, five passes, stopping the moment i becomes 5.

questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: what's the risk when a value falls through an if/else-if chain that has no final else?

options.label: Nothing, as long as the visible cases all work correctly
A value matching none of the conditions can silently fall through with no handling at all
JavaScript automatically adds a default case for you

questions.explanation: A chain with no else produces silence, not an error, when nothing matches — which is exactly what makes an unhandled case dangerous: nothing flags that it happened.

questions.from: Four modules back — Variables and Types
questions.prompt: From Variables and Types: what's the deciding factor in whether a value is a number or a string in JavaScript?

options.label: Whether it has quotes around it
Whether it's made up of digits
How many characters it has

questions.explanation: Quotes decide the type, not the content. "32" in quotes is a string even though it's all digits; 32 with no quotes is a number.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Lists: many values under one name
description: An array holds several values under one name, in a fixed order, indexed starting at 0 — the formal version of the array literals Module 3's loops already ran over without ever explaining how they're built or read.

learningObjectives.text: Create an array literal holding several related values
Read a value out of an array by its index, and read its length
Explain why an array's items are ordered and share one name

contentSections.title: One name, several values, in order

contentSections.body: Module 3's loops already ran over arrays like [200, 400, 100] without ever formally covering what an array actually is or how it's built — this lesson is where that gets made explicit, starting with how one gets written and read.

contentSections.question: Which of these actually holds more than one value under a single name?

options.label: painToday
painThisWeek
painNote

feedback.a: painToday is a single number — one value, one name, nothing to index into.
feedback.b: Right. The square brackets [6, 4, 7, 3, 5] create an array: five separate values, held together under the one name painThisWeek, in a fixed order.
feedback.c: painNote is a single string — one value, even though it's made of several characters, it's not a list of separate items you index into.

contentSections.concept: An **array** is written with square brackets, values separated by commas: `[6, 4, 7, 3, 5]`. It holds several values under one name, in a specific order — the order they were written in, which never rearranges itself on its own.

contentSections.body:
Each value in an array has a position, called its **index**, starting at 0 — not 1. `painThisWeek[0]` is the first value (6), `painThisWeek[1]` is the second (4), and so on. `painThisWeek.length` tells you how many items the array holds — here, 5 — which is also one more than the highest valid index (4).

```
let painThisWeek = [6, 4, 7, 3, 5];
console.log(painThisWeek[0]);      // 6
console.log(painThisWeek.length);  // 5
```
An array holds several values under one name, in order, starting at index 0 — not 1.
A tracker's list of today's symptoms isn't fixed the moment it's written — a new symptom shows up partway through the day, and the array has to be able to grow to hold it.

contentSections.hint: push() adds a new item onto the end of an existing array — it doesn't replace anything already there.
contentSections.answer: The array prints as ["fatigue", "brain fog", "nausea"], and length prints 3. push(...) adds its argument onto the end of the array, growing it by one item — the two original items stay exactly where they were, at index 0 and 1, and "nausea" becomes the new item at index 2.

contentSections.body: `.push(value)` adds a new item onto the end of an array, growing its length by one. It's the most common way an array is built up over time, one item at a time — inside a loop, in response to something happening, or one push at a time as new data arrives. Arrays can also be written directly with everything already in them, the way `painThisWeek` was in the first pod — both are completely normal, and which one you reach for depends on whether you have all the values up front or not.
push(value) adds a new item onto the end of an array without disturbing what's already there.

title: Getting items out, and the index that's off by one
description: The last valid index of an array is always length minus 1, never length itself — and a plain array has no built-in shortcut for "the last item," the way some other languages provide with a negative index.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the last item of an array using its length
Diagnose the off-by-one error caused by using length itself as an index
Explain why a negative index doesn't work in plain JavaScript the way it might elsewhere

contentSections.body: A program needs the most recent pain-level entry — the last item in the array. The obvious-looking line to grab it is also, very reliably, wrong by exactly one.

contentSections.question: This is meant to print the last value in the array (5), but doesn't. What's actually wrong?

options.label: push() should have been used instead of an index
painThisWeek.length is 5, but the last valid index is 4, not 5
Arrays can't be read by index at all, only looped over

feedback.pushwrong: push() adds a new item — it has nothing to do with reading an existing one out. That's not the mismatch here.
feedback.offbyone: Right. length is 5 (the count of items), but indexes start at 0, so the valid indexes are 0 through 4 — index 5 doesn't exist. painThisWeek[5] is undefined, not the last item.
feedback.noindex: Reading by index is completely valid and is exactly how painThisWeek[0] worked in the first lesson — the problem is which index number was used, not whether indexing works at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: length counts items (5 of them); indexes count positions starting from 0 (0, 1, 2, 3, 4). The last valid index is always length - 1, never length itself. painThisWeek[painThisWeek.length] reaches one position past the actual last item — a position that was never assigned anything — so it silently returns undefined instead of throwing an error to flag the mistake.

contentSections.body: The fix is exactly what the error explains: `painThisWeek[painThisWeek.length - 1]` — one less than the count, which lands on the real last index. This specific off-by-one mistake is common enough that it's worth internalizing as its own rule, separate from remembering that indexes start at 0: **the last index is always length minus 1.**
The last valid index is always length - 1, never length itself — a real, common off-by-one mistake.

contentSections.title: There's no shortcut for "the last one" in plain JavaScript

contentSections.body: If you've seen another language, you might expect painThisWeek[-1] to mean "the last item" — a common shortcut elsewhere. In plain JavaScript, it doesn't mean that at all, and knowing that upfront saves a confusing surprise.

contentSections.question: What does this actually print?

options.label: 5 — the last item, counting backward from the end
undefined — plain arrays don't support negative indexes this way
An error, because -1 isn't a valid index

feedback.last: This is exactly the behavior from other languages — but plain JavaScript arrays don't support it. -1 isn't treated as "count from the end" here.
feedback.undef: Right. JavaScript looks for a property literally named "-1" on the array, finds nothing there, and returns undefined — no error, no special "count from the end" behavior.
feedback.error: No error is thrown — JavaScript is quietly permissive about this, not strict. Reading a property (or index) that doesn't exist just returns undefined.

contentSections.mechanism: In plain JavaScript, `array[array.length - 1]` is the standard, reliable way to get the last item — there's no built-in negative-index shortcut for arrays the way some other languages provide. Reaching for [-1] out of habit from another language is a genuinely common mistake, and it fails silently (undefined, no error), which makes it easy to miss.

contentSections.body: Some newer JavaScript methods do support fetching from the end — `array.at(-1)` genuinely does mean "the last item" — but plain square-bracket indexing (`array[-1]`) never does. Until `.at(...)` comes up again later in this track, `array[array.length - 1]` is the dependable way to reach the last item.
array[-1] does not mean "the last item" in JavaScript — use array[array.length - 1] instead.

title: Records: describing one thing with named fields
description: An object holds several named fields describing one thing — read and updated with dot notation, unlike an array, where position is the only label a value gets.

learningObjectives.text: Create an object literal describing one thing with named fields
Read and update a field using dot notation
Explain when an object is a better fit than an array for a given value

contentSections.title: Naming the parts of one thing

contentSections.body: An array is great for many similar values in order — five pain levels, three symptoms. It's a much worse fit for one thing that has several different kinds of information about it: a single medication has a name, a dose, and whether it was taken — three different fields, not five more of the same kind of value.

contentSections.question: What's the actual role of name, doseMg, and takenToday here?

options.label: They're array indexes, like 0, 1, 2
They're field names — labels for each piece of information about this one medication
They're separate, unrelated variables that happen to be written near each other

feedback.indexes: Array indexes are always numbers counting position (0, 1, 2...) — name, doseMg, and takenToday are words describing what each value means, which is a different mechanism entirely.
feedback.fields: Right. This is an object literal — curly braces holding key: value pairs. Each key (name, doseMg, takenToday) labels what its value actually represents, all describing one single medication.
feedback.unrelated: They're deliberately grouped together inside one set of curly braces, all describing the one medication object — not separate variables floating independently.

contentSections.concept: An **object** is written with curly braces, holding `key: value` pairs separated by commas: `{ name: "Ibuprofen", doseMg: 400, takenToday: false }`. Each key is a field name that labels what its value means — unlike an array, where position is the only label a value gets, an object's fields are named, and that name is how you look the value back up.

contentSections.body:
You read a field with dot notation — the object's name, a dot, then the field name:

```
let medication = {
  name: "Ibuprofen",
  doseMg: 400,
  takenToday: false
};

console.log(medication.name);   // "Ibuprofen"
console.log(medication.doseMg); // 400
```

There's no index involved at all — `medication[0]` isn't a thing here, because objects aren't ordered by position the way arrays are. `medication.name` works regardless of which order the fields were written in.
An object's fields are named, not positioned — you look a value up by its field name with a dot, never by an index.
The medication gets taken. takenToday needs to flip from false to true — updating one field of an existing object, without touching the others or rebuilding the whole thing from scratch.

contentSections.scenario: medication currently holds `{ name: "Ibuprofen", doseMg: 400, takenToday: false }`. This line runs: `medication.takenToday = true;`
contentSections.question: Which of these are true about the object after that line runs?

items.label: medication.takenToday is now true
medication.name and medication.doseMg are completely unchanged
A brand-new object was created, separate from the original
The whole object literal had to be rewritten to make this change

explanation.taken_updated: Yes — dot notation on the left of = updates that one field's value directly, the same way reassigning a plain variable does.
explanation.others_unchanged: Yes — updating one field never touches the others. name and doseMg stay exactly as they were.
explanation.new_object: No — this is the same object, modified in place. Nothing new was created; medication still refers to the exact same thing it did before, just with one field changed.
explanation.needs_rewrite: No — that's exactly what dot-notation updating avoids. One targeted line changes one field; the rest of the object is left completely alone.

contentSections.synthesis: medication.takenToday = true updates one field of an existing object in place, the same way spoons = 9 reassigns a plain variable — the difference is that an object holds several named values at once, and dot notation lets you target exactly one of them without disturbing the rest.

contentSections.body: The same dot notation adds a brand-new field that wasn't there originally: `medication.refillDate = "2026-09-01";` adds a fourth field to the object, without anything special needed to "make room" for it. Objects in JavaScript are flexible about their own shape this way — fields can be added or changed after the object already exists, not only at the moment it's first written.
Dot notation both reads and updates a field — object.field = newValue changes just that one field, in place.

title: Lists of records, which is most real data
description: An array of objects reaches a value in two steps — an index to pick the item, a field name to pick the value inside it — and it's the shape almost all real data actually takes.

learningObjectives.text: Build an array of objects describing several similar things
Access a field on a specific item inside an array of objects
Loop over an array of objects, reading a field from each one

contentSections.body: A single medication is an object. A whole medication list is several of those objects, held together in order — which is exactly what an array of objects is, and it's the shape almost all real data actually takes: not one thing, not a flat list of plain values, but many structured things together.

contentSections.question: What does medications[0].doseMg actually reach?

options.label: 400 — the doseMg field of the first object in the array
The whole first object, { name: "Ibuprofen", ... }
An error — you can't mix [0] and .doseMg in one line

feedback.correct: Right. medications[0] reaches the first object in the array (index 0), and .doseMg then reaches that specific object's doseMg field — 400.
feedback.whole_obj: medications[0] alone would give you the whole object — but .doseMg right after it goes one level further, into that specific field.
feedback.error: Combining [0] and .doseMg is completely valid — it's the normal way to reach one field of one item inside an array of objects, read left to right: array index first, then field name.

contentSections.concept: An array of objects combines both shapes you've just learned: `medications[0]` uses an index to reach one item (an object), and `.doseMg` right after it uses a field name to reach one value inside that object. Read left to right, each step narrows further: array → one item → one field.

contentSections.body: An array of objects is reached in two steps: an index to pick the item, then a field name to pick the value inside it.
Module 3's loops walked over arrays of plain numbers. The exact same for...of loop works over an array of objects — the only change is what you do with each item once you have it.

contentSections.hint: On each pass, med is one whole object from the array — the same object medications[0] or medications[1] would have given you directly. What can you do with an object once you have it?
contentSections.answer: "Ibuprofen: 400mg" then "Melatonin: 5mg" — one line per pass. On each pass, med holds one whole object from the array (the first object, then the second), and med.name / med.doseMg reach into that specific object's fields, exactly the way medications[0].name did outside the loop — for...of just hands you each object directly instead of making you index into the array yourself.

contentSections.body: This is the pattern behind most real list-processing code: loop over an array of objects with for...of, and inside the loop, use dot notation on the current item to reach whatever field you need. It's the same loop mechanics from Module 3 — nothing new about the looping itself — combined with the field access from this module's lesson 3.
for...of over an array of objects hands you one whole object per pass — dot notation then reaches the field you need from it.

title: Choosing the right shape for your data
description: Deciding between an array, an object, or an array of objects comes down to what the data actually is, not how many values it has — and parallel arrays that only stay lined up by convention are a common, fragile alternative to getting the shape right.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a set of data is better modeled as an array, an object, or an array of objects
Justify a data-shape choice against a specific real scenario

contentSections.body: A symptom tracker needs to store: today's five pain-level readings, one person's profile (name, age, condition), and a whole week of daily check-ins. All three are "data" — but forcing all three into the same shape produces something clumsy at best and genuinely wrong at worst.

contentSections.scenario: Three things need to be modeled: (1) today's five pain-level readings, taken an hour apart, (2) one person's profile — name, age, primary condition, (3) a full week of daily check-ins, each with a date, a pain level, and a note.
contentSections.question: Which shape fits each one? Select every statement that correctly matches a scenario to its shape.

items.label: Today's five readings fit best as a plain array — [6, 5, 7, 4, 6]
The one profile fits best as a single object — one thing, several named fields
A week of check-ins fits best as an array of objects — several similar things, each with named fields
The profile should be an array, since it has three pieces of information

explanation.readings_array: Yes — five numbers, all the same kind of thing, in a meaningful order (an hour apart). No named fields needed; a plain array is the direct, unforced fit.
explanation.profile_object: Yes — one person, several different kinds of information about them (name, age, condition). That's exactly what an object's named fields are for.
explanation.week_array_of_objects: Yes — several days, each structurally identical (date, pain level, note) but each a separate record. That's an array of objects: many similar things, each with named fields.
explanation.profile_array: No — having several pieces of information isn't what decides array versus object. The profile describes one thing with different kinds of values, which is what named fields (an object) are actually for, regardless of how many fields there are.

contentSections.synthesis: The question to ask isn't "how many values" — it's "is this one thing with several different kinds of information (object), several of the same kind of thing in order (array), or several structured things (array of objects)?" Getting this choice right up front saves a rewrite later, when the data turns out to need fields it was never given room for.

contentSections.body: A useful shortcut: if you'd naturally describe it with "a list of ___", it's probably an array (of a plain value or of objects). If you'd naturally describe it with "a ___ that has a name, a date, a level" — several different labeled facts about one thing — it's probably an object. Most real data ends up being some combination of both, nested inside each other.
Ask what the data actually is before picking a shape: one thing with several fields is an object; several of the same kind of thing is an array.

contentSections.title: Getting it wrong on purpose, to see why

contentSections.body: Someone models a week of check-ins as five separate arrays — one for dates, one for pain levels, one for notes — instead of one array of objects. It runs. It's also a genuinely worse shape, and seeing exactly why is the fastest way to recognize the mistake before making it yourself.

contentSections.question: What's the real problem with modeling it this way instead of as one array of objects?

options.label: Three separate arrays are always slower than one array of objects
Nothing actually keeps the three arrays' matching positions together — sorting or filtering one without the others silently breaks the pairing
JavaScript doesn't allow three arrays to be the same length

feedback.speed: Speed isn't the actual issue here, and for small lists like this it wouldn't be noticeably different either way — the real cost is structural, not performance.
feedback.desync: Right. dates[1], painLevels[1], and notes[1] only describe the same day because you're trusting all three arrays to stay lined up by position — nothing in the code enforces that. Sort painLevels alone, or push a new date without a matching note, and the pairing silently falls apart.
feedback.lengthrule: JavaScript doesn't check or enforce this at all — you could push to one of the three arrays and leave the others unchanged, and nothing would stop you or warn you.

contentSections.mechanism: With three parallel arrays, the relationship between a date, a pain level, and a note exists only in the programmer's head — position 1 of each array happens to describe the same day, purely by convention, with nothing in the code guaranteeing it stays that way. One array of objects — `[{ date: "Mon", painLevel: 6, note: "flare" }, ...]` — keeps each day's three facts physically bundled together in one object, so there's no position to accidentally desynchronize.

contentSections.body: This is the concrete cost of the wrong shape: not that the parallel-arrays version is impossible to use, but that it's fragile in a way that's easy to break without noticing — add, remove, or sort one array and the other two silently stop lining up with it. An array of objects makes that specific mistake structurally impossible, because each day's facts travel together in one object instead of being spread across three separate lists trusting each other to match.
Parallel arrays only stay lined up by convention — nothing enforces it. An array of objects keeps related facts physically bundled together instead.

title: Practice — Restructure Eight Badly-Shaped Datasets
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: reading and updating arrays and objects correctly, and deciding when a dataset needs a different shape than the one it's stuck in.

learningObjectives.text: Predict correct behavior across common array and object operations
Choose the right data shape for a described real-world scenario

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to this module's handful of rules: indexes start at 0 and the last one is length - 1, dot notation reaches a named field, and the shape you pick should match what the data actually is, not just how many values it has.
Almost every data-shape mistake in this module comes down to one question: does this variable hold one thing, or several — and does the code around it agree?

title: Lab — Build a Small Searchable Collection
description: Model a real, personal collection as an array of objects, then write code that filters it down to answer a specific question and sorts it by a field you choose.

learningObjectives.text: Build an array of objects modeling a real, personal collection
Filter the collection to answer a specific real question
Sort the collection by a chosen field

contentSections.body: Every list you've built in this module so far has been small and static. This lab turns that into something closer to a real tool: a collection of your own real records that you can actually search and sort, not just print.

contentSections.title: Build a small searchable collection
contentSections.brief: Pick a real, small collection from your own life — medications, symptoms logged this month, a reading list, a grocery pantry inventory. Model it as an array of objects, each with the same set of named fields, then write code that filters it down to answer a specific question and sorts it by a field you choose.
contentSections.deliverable: A program holding a list of records that can filter and sort them.

stages.title: Model the collection as an array of objects
stages.instructions: Pick your real collection and write it as an array of 5-8 objects, each with the exact same set of 3-4 named fields (for medications: name, doseMg, takenToday, refillDate). Every object in the array needs the same fields, even if some values are placeholders — a consistent shape is what makes filtering and sorting possible in the next stages.
stages.checkpoint: You have an array of 5-8 objects, every one sharing the exact same set of named fields.

stages.title: Filter to answer one real question
stages.instructions: Write a function that takes your array and returns only the items matching one specific condition you actually care about — medications not yet taken today, symptoms above a certain severity, books still unread. Use .filter(...) with a condition that checks one of your fields, and print the filtered result with a labeled console.log.
stages.checkpoint: A function returns a correctly filtered subset of your array, and the filtered result is printed with a clear label.

stages.title: Sort the collection by a field you choose
stages.instructions: Write a second function that returns your array sorted by one of its fields (alphabetically by name, or numerically by a number field). Use .sort(...) with a comparison that matches the field's type — text needs a different comparison than numbers. Print the sorted result, labeled separately from the filtered one.
stages.checkpoint: A function returns your collection sorted correctly by the chosen field, printed with its own clear label, separate from the filtered result.

stages.title: Check both results against the rubric
stages.instructions: Read back through both printed results. Confirm the filtered list only contains items that genuinely match your condition, and the sorted list is actually in the right order from end to end, not just at a glance. Fix anything that doesn't hold up before calling the lab done.
stages.checkpoint: Both the filtered and sorted outputs are independently verified correct, not just visually plausible.

rubric.criterion: The collection is real, personal data, consistently shaped
rubric.meets: 5-8 objects, every one sharing the exact same set of named fields, describing something real from your own life.

rubric.criterion: The filter genuinely answers a specific question
rubric.meets: The filtered output contains only items that actually match a real condition on one of the fields — not the whole list, not an arbitrary subset.

rubric.criterion: The sort is correct end to end
rubric.meets: Every item in the sorted output is in the right position relative to its neighbors, checked past just the first two items.

rubric.criterion: Filtering and sorting are separate functions
rubric.meets: Each is its own named function with one job, not one function doing both at once.

rubric.criterion: Both results are printed and clearly labeled
rubric.meets: Reading the output alone, without the code, makes clear which list is filtered and which is sorted.

contentSections.body: A list of records only becomes a genuinely useful tool once you can ask it something specific — filtering and sorting are the two most common ways to ask.

title: Checkpoint — Lists and Records
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Functions, two reaching back further into Making Decisions and Variables and Types. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

questions.prompt: What's the last valid index of an array with 7 items?
questions.explanation: Indexes start at 0, so 7 items occupy indexes 0 through 6. The last valid index is always length - 1, here 6, not the length itself.

questions.prompt: In `let medication = { doseMg: 400 };`, what does medication.doseMg actually reach?

options.label: The value 400, via the field named doseMg
Index 0 of the object
An error, since objects don't use dot notation

questions.explanation: Objects don't have positional indexes at all — dot notation reaches a value by its field name, doseMg, regardless of the order fields were written in.

questions.prompt: Why is an array of objects usually a better fit than several parallel arrays for a week of check-ins?

options.label: It's always faster to run
It keeps each day's related facts physically bundled together instead of trusting separate arrays to stay lined up by position
JavaScript requires arrays to hold only one type of value

questions.explanation: Parallel arrays only stay matched up by convention — nothing enforces it. An array of objects keeps each record's facts together in one object, making that specific desync mistake structurally impossible.

questions.prompt: What does array[-1] actually return in plain JavaScript?

options.label: The last item, same as in some other languages
undefined — plain arrays don't support this shortcut
The first item

questions.explanation: JavaScript looks for a property literally named "-1", finds nothing, and returns undefined — there's no built-in "count from the end" behavior for plain square-bracket indexing.

questions.prompt: From Functions: what does a function return when it has no return statement at all?

options.label: undefined
Whatever it most recently printed
Calling it throws an error

questions.explanation: Every function call produces a value. With no explicit return statement, that value is always undefined, regardless of what the function printed along the way.

questions.prompt: From Functions: what actually happens when a function is called with a missing argument?

options.label: The call throws an error immediately
The unfilled parameter becomes undefined, and the function keeps running
JavaScript automatically substitutes 0 for any missing argument

questions.explanation: A missing argument doesn't error — the parameter it would have filled simply becomes undefined, unless a default value was explicitly written for it.

questions.prompt: From Functions: what's the real difference between console.log(...) inside a function and return?

options.label: console.log displays a value; return hands a value back to the code that called the function
They're interchangeable — both make the value usable afterward
return is only for numbers, console.log is for everything else

questions.explanation: Displaying a value and handing it back to the caller are two separate actions. Only return makes a function's result usable by whatever called it.

questions.prompt: From Functions: what's a strong signal, in a function's own name, that it might be doing more than one job?

options.label: It contains "and", joining two separate verbs
It's longer than eight characters
It takes more than one parameter

questions.explanation: A name honestly describing one job rarely needs "and" — a name like validateAndSaveEntry is confessing, in its own text, that it's doing at least two separate things.

questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: what's the risk when a value falls through an if/else-if chain that has no final else?

options.label: A value matching none of the conditions can silently fall through with no handling at all
JavaScript throws an error automatically
The first branch runs by default

questions.explanation: A chain with no else produces silence, not an error, when nothing matches — which is exactly what makes an unhandled case dangerous: nothing flags that it happened.

questions.from: Four modules back — Variables and Types
questions.prompt: From Variables and Types: why does "5" === 5 come out false in JavaScript?

options.label: === always returns false when a number is involved
One is a string and one is a number — different types, even with matching digits
5 needs a decimal point to count as a real number

questions.explanation: === checks type as well as value. "5" (a string) and 5 (a number) hold the "same" digits but are different types, so they're not equal.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.
